# Introduction

In order to fulfill the requirement of the assignment I have followed the following steps:

## Stage 1: Account Registration and API Key Acquisition

- **What I have done:** Setting up my access pass to the NYT database and creating the login at <https://developer.nytimes.com/>.

- Click **+ New App**. Give my app a name as "Book API", enabled the **Books API** product, and click **Save**. Click on my newly created app from the list and copy the generated **API Key** string and Kept this handy; As I will need it for Stage 2.

## Stage 2: Secure Credential Management

- **What I have done:** Ensuring my private API key is hidden from plain text so that my code remains secure and reproducible (especially if you push your code to GitHub).

- For that purpose, opened my R console and ran usethis::edit_r_environ() to open mylocal .Renviron file. where I added my key.

- Save the file and restart my R session.

- In my Quarto document, I will later pull this key dynamically via Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY") rather than typing the key out explicitly.

## Stage 3: Defining the Analytical Question

What have done: Framing my data goals before writing code so my report tells a clear, cohesive story.

- **Selected Endpoint**: The NYT Books API Hardcover Fiction current list (\[https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/current/hardcover-fiction.json\]

- **Research Question**: "Which publishers dominate the current New York Times Hardcover Fiction bestseller list, and how do their publication trends break down by ranking and longevity (weeks on the list)?"

- Writing this out clearly in the introductory text section of my Quarto document satisfies the requirement to ask and attempt to answer an interesting question.

## Stage 4: Data Acquisition and Parsing

**What I have done**: Submitting an automated request from R to the NYT server, pulling down the raw JSON package, and translating it into an R-readable object.

- In my Quarto code blocks, I will first load libraries (httr, jsonlite, tidyverse, janitor) in chunk 1.

- I will construct my request URL dynamically by combining the endpoint base URL with my environment variable (Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY")).

- I will pass that URL into jsonlite::fromJSON(..., flatten = TRUE). This converts the incoming nested JSON text file into an R list structure.

## Stage 5: Tidying and Data Cleaning

- **What I have done**: Extracting the specific table of books from the broader JSON list payload, cleaning up formatting, handling missing structural pieces, and turning it into a tidy tibble ready for visualization.

- Access the inner dataframe by navigating through the list structure: response \$results\$books.

- Convert it to a tidy tibble (as_tibble()).

- Standardizing column headers using janitor::clean_names() (which converts everything to lower-case snake_case like weeks_on_list or rank_last_week).

- Selecting only the variables I needed for my analysis (e.g., rank, title, author, publisher, weeks_on_list).

Now lets see the code /chunks one by one

## 1. Load Required Libraries

The following chunk loads the essential packages needed for HTTP requests, JSON parsing, and data manipulation.

```{r Check 1 Setup and Libraries, Warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Chunk 1: Setup and Libraries
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

## 2. Securely Retrieve the API Key

This chunk verifies that my API key is correctly loaded from my environment variables without exposing sensitive credentials in plain text.

```{r Check 2 API Authentication Check, Warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

nyt_api_key <- Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY")

if (nyt_api_key == "") {
  stop("Error: NYT_API_KEY environment variable is not set. Please configure your .Renviron file.")
} else {
  message("API key successfully loaded from environment variables.")
}
```

## 3. Construct Request URL and Fetch Data

Here, I target the current Hardcover Fiction bestseller list endpoint and parse the JSON response.

```{r Check 3 Make Request and Parse JSON, Warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

base_url <- "https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/current/hardcover-fiction.json"
request_url <- paste0(base_url, "?api-key=", nyt_api_key)

# Fetch and parse JSON response
response <- fromJSON(request_url, flatten = TRUE)

# Inspect the top-level structure of the response list
print(response$status)
```

## 4. Extract and Transform Nested Data into a Tidy Tibble

The raw response embeds book attributes deep inside a nested dataframe list. This chunk extracts those rows and structures them into a tidy tibble.

```{r Check 4 Extract and Clean Data Frame, Warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

nyt_books_df <- response$results$books %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(
    rank,
    rank_last_week,
    weeks_on_list,
    title,
    author,
    publisher,
    description,
    primary_isbn13
  ) %>%
  rename(isbn13 = primary_isbn13)

# View the first few rows of the clean dataset
head(nyt_books_df)
```

## 5. Data Cleaning Documentation & Summary Statistics

**Data Cleaning Notes:**

**Nested Fields:** The primary data table returned by the NYT API nested individual book metadata inside a books list frame. I extracted this sub-element directly using pipe operations.

**Missing Values:** rank_last_week defaults to 0 or NA for books newly entering the bestseller list. These were retained as-is to preserve list entry status.

**Naming Conventions**: Standardized column names to lowercase snake_case using janitor::clean_names().

```{r Check 5 Summary Statistics on Publishers, Warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

publisher_summary <- nyt_books_df %>% 
  group_by(publisher) %>%
  summarise(
    total_books = n(),
    avg_weeks_on_list = mean(weeks_on_list, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_books))

print(publisher_summary)
```

## 6: Data Visualization

This chunk satisfies the analytical visualization requirement by plotting publisher frequency or ranking distribution on the current bestseller list.

```{r Check 6 Visualization of Top Publishers, Warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}


ggplot(publisher_summary, aes(x = reorder(publisher, total_books), y = total_books)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c3e50") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Bestseller Distribution by Publisher",
    subtitle = "Current NYT Hardcover Fiction List",
    x = "Publisher",
    y = "Number of Bestselling Titles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```
